```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.2, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
```

Calibrations are usually judged by how well they simulate a whole record from rain alone. A
forecasting model does something else. Every few hours it is updated with the latest observed
flow and asked what happens next, over a few hours to a day or two. A model that simulates the
record a little worse may forecast better, because the updating corrects what it gets wrong and
it gets the shape of the next few hours right. The fair test of a forecasting model is to make
it forecast.

# Hindcasts

A hindcast replays the past as if it were live: from regular points in the record (the
origins), the model is updated with the flow observed so far and run forward, and its forecast
is compared with what then happened. `pdm_hindcast()` does this with several updating methods
at once, and with persistence, the forecast that the flow stays as it is now. `skill` is one
minus the forecast's mean squared error over persistence's: 1 is perfect, 0 no better than
assuming nothing changes.

# Three candidates

The synthetic catchment of [Counting every error fairly](fair-errors.html), and three candidate
models: the truth, a calibration by NSE, and a model whose surface store is three times too slow.

```{r data}
rain <- synthetic_rain("2017-10-01", years = 3, dt = 1, seed = 5)
truth <- modifyList(pdm_presets("standard"), list(area_km2 = 25))
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
forcing <- rain[c("time", "rain", "pet")]
set.seed(8)
flow <- run_pdm(model, forcing[c("rain", "pet")], initial_state(model, 0.5))$output$q_m3s
observed <- flow * exp(rnorm(length(flow), 0, 0.15))
start <- modifyList(truth, list(fc = 0.8))
fit <- calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower = c(fc = 0.6, surface.k1 = 1),
                     upper = c(fc = 1.4, surface.k1 = 30), warmup = 24 * 90, start = "soil",
                     control = list(maxit = 40))
slow <- truth
slow$surface$k1 <- truth$surface$k1 * 3
candidates <- list(truth = model, calibrated = fit$model, slow = pdm_from_config(slow))
```

# Ranking by skill

`compare_forecasts()` hindcasts every candidate alike and ranks them by mean skill over the
lead times that matter. Each is judged with its best updating method at each lead, as it would be
run.

```{r compare}
cmp <- compare_forecasts(candidates, forcing, observed, horizon_h = 12, every_h = 6,
                         leads_h = c(1, 3, 6, 12), ar = list(ea = ar_ea_default()))
cmp
plot(cmp)
```

Three things stand out. The skill rises with the lead, because persistence gets worse faster
than the models do: a river rarely stays as it is for twelve hours. The truth and the calibrated
model are equal, 0.891 against 0.892; a difference that small is noise, and the ranking puts
the calibration first only by chance. And the model with the slow surface store is worse than
persistence at an hour ahead (skill below zero): it is late on every rise, which matters most at
the shortest leads. Over the whole record its simulation is not far off; as a forecaster it is
plainly the worst.

The lead at which a candidate's skill falls towards zero is where it stops earning its keep; a
model below zero at the leads the service uses should not be used there.

# Ranking by warnings

For flood warning, what matters most is whether the forecast crosses the threshold when the
river does, and not when it does not. With `thresholds`, each lead also gets the probability of
detection, the false alarm ratio and the critical success index, and `rank_on = "threshold"`
ranks by one of them.

```{r threshold}
high <- c(high = unname(stats::quantile(observed, 0.99)))
warn <- compare_forecasts(candidates, forcing, observed, horizon_h = 12, every_h = 6,
                          leads_h = c(3, 6, 12), ar = list(ea = ar_ea_default()),
                          thresholds = high, rank_on = "threshold")
warn$ranking
```

The critical success index counts hits over hits, misses and false alarms together: 1 is
perfect. A model can rank differently on skill and on warnings; for a flood warning service the
warnings decide.

# One updating method for all

`method = "none"` judges every candidate open loop, with no updating: the model alone. That
separates what the model knows from what the updating repairs, and shows how much each candidate
leans on the updating.

```{r open-loop}
compare_forecasts(candidates, forcing, observed, horizon_h = 12, every_h = 6,
                  leads_h = c(1, 3, 6, 12), method = "none", ar = list())$ranking
```

Here the open-loop scores are the same as the best ones: no updating method beat the model alone
at any lead. The errors in this made-up record are random from hour to hour, so correcting the
forecast towards the latest, noisy, observation does not help. Real errors persist for hours, and
there updating usually wins at the short leads; comparing the two rankings shows by how much.

# Cautions

- **Hindcasts use the observed rain.** A real forecast uses forecast rain, which adds its own
  error and grows with the lead. Hindcast skill is the model's part of the forecast's skill.
- **Judge on the lead times the service uses.** A model best at one hour and worst at six is
  the wrong model for a catchment that needs six hours' warning.
- **Use the validation years, or the test years,** not the calibration years, for the final
  choice.
